claims.text: The starting material consists of sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
The nanoparticles were synthesized by pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane.
The as-deposited AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are initially single-phase FCC.
The initial nanoparticles have elliptical or icosahedral geometry.
Au and Cu have lower surface energies than Co, Ni, and Pt.
Surface-energy anisotropy creates chemical-potential gradients that preferentially segregate Au and Cu to the nanoparticle surface.
For particles below 10 nm, the high surface-to-volume ratio makes the surface-energy contribution to Gibbs free energy dominant.
Bulk Gibbs-free-energy models commonly neglect the surface-energy term important to sub-10 nm particles.
The surface-energy driving force produces rapid surface diffusion despite the nominal sluggish-diffusion behavior of high-entropy alloys.
Element-selective transport and loss can remain active in a high-entropy alloy rather than being eliminated by sluggish diffusion.
Surface-segregated Au and Cu have higher vapor pressures and lower binding energies, causing them to evaporate preferentially.
Preferential Au/Cu evaporation reduces nanoparticle volume and causes coalescence of the remaining particles.
Surface segregation, evaporation, and coalescence reshape elliptical or icosahedral particles into spherical particles.
Approximately 600 K is the critical temperature above which Au/Cu surface segregation and evaporation become dominant.
Above the critical temperature, Au/Cu segregation and evaporation become faster than bulk diffusion.
The mechanism will produce measurable particle-mass loss, a wider size distribution, and a transition from elliptical to spherical morphology.
Surface-energy gradients alone can reproduce phase separation without reducing configurational entropy.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to particles smaller than 10 nm.
For particles larger than 50 nm, bulk sluggish diffusion should dominate and prevent rapid segregation and evaporation.
The critical temperature depends on initial stoichiometry and defects such as stacking faults because these can alter surface-diffusion barriers.
